options.label: A human absorbs a codebase's patterns gradually over time; an agent starts every task with zero accumulated context unless something explicitly loads it
Agents are structurally incapable of using search tools
This isn't actually different for agents versus humans

questions.explanation: Lesson one's second pod — an agent has no gradual, ambient familiarity with a codebase the way a human contributor develops over time, so the read-first step has to be deliberate and enforced.

questions.prompt: What should a verify step return on failure, beyond a bare pass/fail boolean?

options.label: The actual failure output and failed test names, so the agent can diagnose the cause instead of guessing at a different attempt
Nothing more is needed — a boolean is sufficient information
Just a retry count

questions.explanation: Lesson two's second pod — a bare boolean produces blind, undirected retries; real failure detail lets the agent diagnose before trying again.

questions.prompt: Why is an automated scope check ('does this diff match its expected scope') more reliable at scale than trusting a human reviewer to catch scope creep by eyeballing every diff?

options.label: Human attention doesn't stay consistently sharp across every single diff at volume, while an automated first pass triages consistently regardless of time of day or fatigue
Humans are structurally incapable of ever noticing scope creep
It isn't more reliable — eyeballing is just as effective at any volume

questions.explanation: Lesson four's second pod — the same logic as the test-file guardrail: anything depending on consistent human attention across high volume isn't reliable at scale, so an automated check triages it instead.

title: Processing a thousand items reliably
description: Why a design that works fine for a handful of agent calls falls over at real volume — rate limits, bounded concurrency, and what 'reliable at scale' actually requires.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why sequential, unbounded-retry processing fails at real batch volume
Design a batch processor with bounded concurrency and rate-limit-aware retry

contentSections.title: What works for ten calls doesn't work for a thousand

contentSections.body: A team's single-task research agent works great — a handful of API calls per run, nothing ever throttled. They reuse the same pattern to process 1,000 support tickets overnight: one call per ticket, sequentially, no rate-limit handling because it never came up before. By ticket 340, every call is failing with a 429. The job silently hangs until someone notices the next morning.

contentSections.scenario: Nothing about the per-ticket logic itself was wrong — the same code processed the first 300 tickets fine.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism behind the failure at scale?

options.label: The design never accounted for provider rate limits, which only become a real constraint at volumes far higher than a typical single-task agent ever reaches
The model gets less accurate the more calls are made in a session
Ticket 340 specifically must have contained something malformed

feedback.rate-limit: Right. A handful of calls never brushes up against a provider's rate limit — 1,000 sequential calls with no backoff logic runs straight into it, and nothing about the per-item logic needed to be wrong for this to happen.
feedback.accuracy: There's no mechanism by which making more calls degrades the model's accuracy on later calls — each call is independent. The failure here is entirely about request volume hitting a hard limit, not quality drifting.
feedback.bad-item: The pattern (every call failing from ticket 340 onward, not just one) points at a systemic constraint being hit, not a single bad ticket — a malformed item would fail on its own call, not cause every subsequent call to fail too.

contentSections.mechanism: Rate limits are a real, hard constraint every major API provider enforces, and they only become visible at volumes a typical single-task agent (a handful of calls per run) never reaches. A design proven at 10 calls tells you nothing about whether it survives 1,000 — the failure mode literally doesn't exist until volume crosses a threshold nobody tested against.

contentSections.body:
This is the first thing batch and workflow agents have that single-task agents mostly don't: real exposure to volume-driven constraints. Two design choices matter immediately:

1. **Bounded concurrency** — not fully sequential (too slow, and doesn't actually avoid rate limits if retries pile up) and not fully parallel (guarantees hitting the rate limit almost immediately). A worker pool of maybe 5-10 concurrent calls pulling from a shared queue is a reasonable middle ground for most providers' limits.
2. **Rate-limit-aware retry** — when a 429 comes back, back off and retry *that specific call*, rather than letting it crash the whole batch or hammering the API again immediately.

Neither of these matters at 10 calls. Both are close to mandatory at 1,000.

A design proven at a handful of calls tells you nothing about whether it survives real batch volume — rate limits are a constraint that only becomes visible once you cross a threshold most single-task agents never reach.

contentSections.title: Building the worker pool

contentSections.body: A second team fixes the rate-limit crash by adding a retry — but retries every failure the same way, including a genuinely malformed ticket that will never succeed no matter how many times it's retried. The batch spends twenty minutes retrying one broken item before anyone notices the other 999 are just waiting.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: should a rate-limit error (429) and a malformed-input error be retried the same way?
contentSections.answer: No — a rate-limit error is transient and worth retrying with backoff, but a malformed item will fail identically on every retry, so it should be recorded as a failure and skipped, not retried indefinitely.
contentSections.hint: One of these errors is about timing (try again later); the other is about the item itself never being processable as-is.

contentSections.body: Not every failure deserves the same response — a transient rate limit is worth retrying with backoff, but a malformed item will fail the same way every time and should be recorded and skipped instead.

title: Per-item failure without losing the batch
description: Why one item's failure shouldn't take down 499 others' worth of work, and how persisted per-item status turns a crash-and-restart into a resume.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why per-item failure isolation matters more than batch-level error handling
Design persisted per-item status tracking that lets a batch resume after a crash

contentSections.title: One bad item, 499 lost results

contentSections.body: A 500-item batch throws an unhandled exception on item 240 — nothing wraps the per-item work in a try/catch, so the exception propagates all the way up and kills the whole job. The 239 items that already succeeded are gone; nothing was saved. The team reruns the whole batch from scratch.

contentSections.scenario: Two ways an unhandled item-level error could be treated.
contentSections.question: Which is the better default for a batch job?

options.label: Catch the failure at the item level, record it, and let the batch continue processing the remaining items
Let any single item's error propagate and abort the whole batch, since something clearly went wrong

feedback.isolate: Right. One item failing is usually a fact about that item, not a signal the whole batch is compromised — isolating it preserves everything that already succeeded and lets the batch keep making progress.
feedback.abort-all: This treats a single item's failure as if it invalidates the other 499 items' worth of work, which is rarely true and is expensive when it isn't — a genuinely systemic failure (the API itself is down) is a different, much rarer case that does warrant stopping.

contentSections.concept: Per-item failure isolation: wrap each item's processing in its own error boundary, record the outcome (success or failure, with detail) per item, and keep the batch moving. A batch-wide abort should be reserved for evidence of a genuinely systemic problem — not the default response to one bad item among hundreds.

contentSections.body: A single item's failure is usually a fact about that item, not the whole batch — isolate it at the item level so 499 other results don't get thrown away over one bad one.

contentSections.title: Resuming instead of restarting

contentSections.body: Isolation alone still leaves a gap: if the whole *process* crashes (not just one item's logic — the machine restarts, an unhandled exception in the harness itself, a deploy interrupts it), all the in-memory results from items 1-339 are gone the moment the process dies, even though none of that logic ever failed.

contentSections.scenario: Before seeing the real pattern: for a 500-item batch that crashes and restarts at item 340, without any persisted status, roughly what fraction of the already-completed work is typically lost?
contentSections.question: Your estimate — what fraction of the 339 already-processed items is lost on an in-memory-only restart?
contentSections.explanation: All of it — 100%. If status only lives in memory, a process crash erases it completely regardless of how much progress was made; the restart has no way to know item 1 through 339 were already handled, so it reprocesses (and re-pays for) every one of them.

contentSections.body: In-memory progress dies with the process — persisting per-item status is what turns a crash from 'lose everything, restart from zero' into 'resume exactly where it left off.'

title: Validating output at volume
description: Why 'the JSON parsed' is a much weaker check than it sounds, and how structural validation and semantic plausibility catch different, both-necessary categories of bad output.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish structural validity from semantic plausibility in extracted output
Build a validation function that checks both, with specific per-field failure detail

contentSections.title: Valid JSON, nonsense values

contentSections.body: A pipeline extracts structured data from 2,000 scanned receipts — name, email, order total. Validation is one check: does the output parse as JSON with the right keys? It does, for all 2,000. One of them is `{"name": "J0hn Sm1th", "email": "noemail", "total": -45.20}`. It passed.

contentSections.question: What's the actual gap in this validation function?

options.label: It only checks that the required keys exist with some value — it never checks whether those values are actually plausible (a valid-looking email, a non-negative total)
It's missing a check for whether the record is valid JSON in the first place
It should check more fields, not just three

feedback.structural-only: Right. This function answers 'are the required keys present with some value,' which `-45.20` and `'noemail'` both satisfy — it never asks whether those specific values make sense for what they're supposed to represent.
feedback.json-parse: By the time a record reaches this function, it's already a parsed object — JSON-parse failure is a separate, earlier failure mode this function isn't meant to catch, and adding that check wouldn't touch the actual gap here.
feedback.more-fields: Checking more fields the same shallow way (presence only) wouldn't catch a negative total or a malformed email either — the problem isn't which fields are checked, it's what 'checked' means.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix isn't more required fields — it's a second layer of checking, on top of presence: does the email actually look like an email, is the total a sensible non-negative number, does the date fall in a plausible range. Structural validity (right shape) and semantic plausibility (right kind of value) are two different questions, and a real validation layer has to answer both.

contentSections.body: Structural validity (right shape) and semantic plausibility (right kind of value) are different checks — at volume, whatever a validation layer doesn't explicitly check for ships silently, unreviewed by anyone.

contentSections.title: What a good validator returns

contentSections.body: A second validator does check semantic plausibility — but returns just `false` on any failure, with no indication of which field or why. A human reviewing 60 failures out of 2,000 has to manually re-inspect every single one to find out what actually went wrong before they can fix anything.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: should a validation function's failure output be a bare boolean, or something more?
contentSections.answer: Something more — a list of which specific field(s) failed and why, so a reviewer or a retry step can act on the failure directly instead of re-deriving what went wrong from scratch for every single failed record.
contentSections.hint: This is the same principle from this track's coding-agents module — what a verify step should return on failure, applied here to data validation.

contentSections.body: A validation failure is only as useful as the detail it carries — a bare false forces every downstream consumer to re-derive what went wrong; specific, per-field reasons let a batch of failures actually be triaged.

title: Agents that trigger real-world actions
description: Why an action with a real-world side effect needs a dry-run gate and an idempotency check that a purely internal computation doesn't.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish real-world side-effecting actions from safe-to-retry internal computation
Explain why idempotency specifically protects against duplicate real-world side effects on retry

contentSections.title: Not every action is safe to just retry

contentSections.body: A workflow agent sends confirmation emails as the final step of a 500-item batch. It crashes mid-run and restarts. The restart logic (from lesson two) correctly resumes from where it left off for computation — but the email-sending step doesn't check whether an email was already sent for a given item before the crash. 150 customers get two confirmation emails.

contentSections.scenario: The per-item status tracking from lesson two was in place and working correctly for tracking computation.
contentSections.question: What's the actual gap that let duplicate emails go out?

options.label: The side-effecting action itself (sending the email) didn't check whether it had already happened for this item — status tracking covered computation progress, not whether the external action had fired
The per-item status tracking from lesson two doesn't work and needs to be redesigned
Email sending is inherently unreliable and duplicates are unavoidable

feedback.no-idempotency: Right. Status tracking correctly knew which items had been *processed* — but 'processed' and 'the email was actually sent' can diverge if the crash happened between those two steps, or if the check covered one but not the other.
feedback.tracking-broken: The tracking mechanism itself worked fine for its actual job — resuming computation. The gap is specific to the side-effecting action not having its own dedicated check, not a flaw in the tracking system generally.
feedback.unavoidable: Duplicate side effects on retry are a well-understood, preventable problem — idempotency keys and pre-action checks exist specifically to prevent this, it's not an unavoidable cost of automation.

contentSections.mechanism: A real-world side effect (an email sent, a charge issued, a refund processed) is fundamentally different from an internal computation: redoing a computation from the same inputs produces the same harmless result, but redoing a side effect produces a *second* real-world event. Status tracking for computation progress and a dedicated idempotency check for the side effect itself are two different safeguards, and having one doesn't substitute for the other.

contentSections.body: Computation is safe to redo; a real-world side effect is not — it needs its own dedicated idempotency check immediately before it fires, separate from whatever tracks computation progress.

contentSections.title: The gate before the first real run

contentSections.body: A team builds a workflow agent that auto-approves refunds under a threshold for a backlog of 300 flagged orders. Before ever running it for real, someone asks: what does this actually do, across all 300, before we let it touch real money?

contentSections.question: Before reading on: what should happen before a batch of real-world side-effecting actions runs 'for real' the first time?
contentSections.answer: A dry run — the agent computes and reports exactly what it *would* do for every item (which refunds, for how much), without actually issuing anything, so a human can review the full scope before any real-world action fires.
contentSections.hint: Idempotency protects against re-running an action that already happened. What protects against a batch of real actions being wrong the first time, before any of them have happened yet?

contentSections.body: Idempotency protects a side effect from happening twice; a dry-run gate protects it from happening wrong the first time — a batch of real-world actions needs both, not just one.

title: Reporting on a batch a human must review
description: Why an aggregate count isn't a report a human can act on, and what per-item detail a batch review actually needs.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a batch report gives a human reviewer enough detail to act on the results
Design a batch review report structure covering successes, failures, and borderline cases

contentSections.title: Two numbers aren't a report

contentSections.body: A 1,000-item batch finishes and reports: 'succeeded: 940, failed: 60.' A reviewer opens it needing to know what to actually do next, and the report has nothing else — not which 60, not why, not whether any of the 940 'successes' are worth a second look.

contentSections.scenario: Before a batch report is considered done, what does it actually need to contain for a human to act on it?
contentSections.question: Which of these does a genuinely useful batch review report require?

items.label: Each failure listed individually with its specific reason
An aggregate success/fail count, as the primary content
A separate bucket for items that passed validation but are worth a second look (e.g. low-confidence)
For any item that triggered a real-world action, a clear record of exactly what happened
A success percentage instead of raw counts

explanation.per-failure-detail: This is what actually lets a reviewer act — 'which 60, and why' is the difference between a report and a headline.
explanation.aggregate-only: A count is a fine summary at the top of a report, but useless as the entire report — it tells a reviewer nothing about what to do next.
explanation.borderline-cases: Items that technically passed but deserve a second look are easy to lose entirely if a report only distinguishes pass/fail — this bucket is what keeps them visible.
explanation.side-effect-record: Anything that touched the real world (a refund issued, an email sent) deserves its own explicit record — a reviewer shouldn't have to guess what actually happened versus what was merely attempted.
explanation.percentage-only: Swapping a count for a percentage doesn't add any of the missing detail — it's the same problem in different units.

contentSections.synthesis: A genuinely useful report separates clear successes, clear failures (each with a specific reason), and a borderline bucket worth a second look — plus an explicit record of any real-world side effect that fired. An aggregate number, in any form, is a headline for this report, not a substitute for it.

contentSections.body: A batch pipeline generates rich per-item detail at every stage — a good report's only job is not throwing that detail away by collapsing everything into an aggregate count.

contentSections.title: Designing the report before running the batch

contentSections.body: A team builds their report structure only after a batch finishes and a reviewer complains it's useless — by then, the pipeline never captured the per-item detail (confidence scores, specific validation errors) that would have made a good report possible, because nobody planned for it upfront.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: should a batch report's structure be designed before or after the pipeline that generates the data it needs?
contentSections.answer: Before — a report can only surface detail the pipeline actually captured along the way, so the report's requirements (per-field error reasons, confidence scores, side-effect records) need to shape what each stage logs from the start.
contentSections.hint: Can a report show a confidence score or a specific error reason if nothing upstream ever recorded it?

contentSections.body: This is a design-order point, not just a formatting one: a report can only ever surface what the pipeline captured on the way there. If lesson three's validator only returned a bare boolean, no report downstream can retroactively produce field-level failure reasons — that detail simply doesn't exist anywhere by the time reporting happens. Designing the report's requirements *first* — what does a reviewer need to see, per item — and working backward to what each stage needs to log is what makes a genuinely useful report possible, rather than a post-hoc patch on top of data that was never rich enough to support it.

A report can only show what the pipeline actually captured — design what a reviewer needs to see first, and let that shape what each stage logs, rather than trying to patch a report onto data that was never detailed enough.

title: Design batch handling for seven workflows
description: Seven drills applying this module's full toolkit — bounded concurrency, per-item isolation, layered validation, idempotent side effects, and reviewable reporting — to new batch and workflow scenarios.

learningObjectives.text: Apply concurrency, isolation, validation, idempotency, and reporting judgment to new batch and workflow scenarios

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: No new concepts here — the same toolkit from the five lessons, run against batch and workflow scenarios you haven't seen yet.

The habit worth keeping: before trusting a batch or workflow agent's results, ask whether it handled volume without hitting rate limits, isolated per-item failures, validated output beyond mere structure, protected real-world actions with idempotency, and produced a report you can actually act on.

title: Build a batch agent with validation
description: Build a 500-item batch agent with bounded concurrency, per-item resumability, layered validation, and a reviewable report.

learningObjectives.text: Build a reliable batch-processing agent with per-item validation and a human-actionable review report

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every technique in this module — bounded concurrency, per-item isolation and resumability, layered validation, idempotent side effects, and a reviewable report — was building toward one concrete proof: an agent that processes 500 items reliably, with a report a human could actually act on.

contentSections.title: An agent processing 500 items with per-item outcomes
contentSections.brief: Build a batch agent that processes 500 items (real or synthetic data — e.g. extracting structured fields from 500 short text records, or classifying 500 items into categories). It must use bounded concurrency with rate-limit-aware retry, persist per-item status so it can resume after a simulated crash, validate every output both structurally and semantically, and produce a review report a human could act on without re-investigating each failure from scratch.
contentSections.deliverable: Working batch-processing code; a persisted per-item status store that survives and correctly resumes from a simulated mid-batch crash; a validation layer with structural and semantic checks; and a final review report with per-item failure detail, a borderline/needs-review bucket, and correct summary counts.

stages.title: Build bounded, resumable processing
stages.instructions: Implement the worker pool with bounded concurrency and rate-limit-aware retry (lesson one). Add persisted per-item status tracking (lesson two). Run the batch partway, then simulate a crash (kill the process or stop it manually) and restart — confirm it resumes from where it left off rather than reprocessing completed items.
stages.checkpoint: A demonstrated resume from a simulated crash — logged proof that already-succeeded items were skipped, not reprocessed.

stages.title: Add layered validation
stages.instructions: Build a validator that checks both structural correctness (right shape, right types) and semantic plausibility (values that make sense for what they represent) on every item's output (lesson three). Run the full 500-item batch to completion with validation applied to every result.
stages.checkpoint: All 500 items processed and validated, with specific per-field failure reasons recorded for anything that failed either layer of validation.

stages.title: Build the review report
stages.instructions: Produce a final report with: accurate summary counts, a per-item failure list with specific reasons, and a needs-review bucket for anything that passed validation but scored low on some confidence or plausibility signal you define. If any part of your batch triggers an external action, confirm it's protected by an idempotency check (lesson four) and reflected explicitly in the report.
stages.checkpoint: A complete review report a human could act on directly — not just aggregate counts — covering successes, specific failures, and any borderline cases.

rubric.criterion: Processing is bounded and rate-limit-aware
rubric.meets: Concurrency is limited (not fully sequential, not fully parallel), and rate-limit errors specifically trigger backoff-and-retry.

rubric.criterion: The batch genuinely resumes after a crash
rubric.meets: A real, demonstrated restart shows already-completed items being skipped, not a claim that the design would support it.

rubric.criterion: Validation checks structure and semantics separately
rubric.meets: Both layers are implemented and distinguishable in the failure output — a type error and a plausibility error are reported differently.

rubric.criterion: Any real-world side effect is idempotency-protected
rubric.meets: If the batch triggers an external action, a check prevents it from firing twice for the same item on retry or resume.

rubric.criterion: The report is genuinely actionable
rubric.meets: A reviewer could act on specific failures and borderline cases directly from the report, without re-running or re-investigating each one from scratch.

contentSections.body: A batch agent earns trust the same way a coding agent's merge gate does — not by claiming it handles volume and failure gracefully, but by a demonstrated crash-and-resume and a report specific enough to actually be used.

title: Checkpoint — Data and Workflow Agents
description: Ungraded retrieval: 4 from this module, 4 from Coding Agents (the previous module in this phase), 2 from further back in Research Agents.

learningObjectives.text: Recall this module's batch-and-workflow vocabulary and reconnect it to coding-agent guardrails and research-agent verification from earlier in this phase

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Data and Workflow Agents
contentSections.framing: No grade, no timer. Answer from memory before scrolling back.

questions.from: This module — Data and Workflow Agents
questions.prompt: Why does a design proven at a handful of API calls tell you nothing about whether it survives 1,000 sequential calls?

options.label: Provider rate limits are a real constraint that only becomes visible at volumes far higher than a typical single-task agent reaches
The model becomes less accurate as call count increases
It always does survive — volume has no effect on reliability

questions.explanation: Lesson one — rate limits are invisible at small scale and become a hard constraint at real batch volume, regardless of whether the per-item logic itself is correct.

questions.from: This module — Data and Workflow Agents
questions.prompt: Why should one item's failure in a 500-item batch be isolated rather than aborting the whole batch?

options.label: A single item's failure is usually a fact about that item, not evidence the other 499 items' work is compromised
Batch-wide abort is always the safer, more correct default
Isolating failures is only useful for very large batches, not moderate ones

questions.explanation: Lesson two — per-item isolation preserves already-completed work; a batch-wide abort should be reserved for genuinely systemic failure, not the default response to one bad item.

questions.from: This module — Data and Workflow Agents
questions.prompt: Why does 'the output parsed as valid JSON with the right keys' fail to catch a negative order total or a malformed email?

options.label: Structural validity (right shape) and semantic plausibility (right kind of value) are different checks, and parsing only confirms the first
It doesn't fail to catch these — valid JSON parsing is sufficient on its own
JSON parsing is unrelated to data validation entirely

questions.explanation: Lesson three — a record can be structurally valid JSON with the right keys while containing values that are semantically nonsense; both layers of checking are needed.

questions.from: This module — Data and Workflow Agents
questions.prompt: Why does a real-world side effect (an email sent, a refund issued) need its own idempotency check, separate from per-item computation-status tracking?

options.label: Redoing a computation is harmless, but redoing a side effect creates a second real-world event — the two need independent protection
Computation-status tracking already covers this automatically
Idempotency only matters for financial actions, not for things like emails

questions.explanation: Lesson four — computation is safe to redo; an external side effect is not, since each redo is a genuinely new real-world event, which is why it needs its own dedicated check.

questions.from: This module — Data and Workflow Agents
questions.prompt: Why is 'succeeded: 940, failed: 60' not a complete batch review report?

options.label: It gives a reviewer no way to know which 60 failed, why, or which of the 940 successes deserve a second look
It is complete — a reviewer only needs the aggregate numbers to decide what to do
It's incomplete only because it uses raw counts instead of percentages

questions.explanation: Lesson five — an aggregate count is a headline, not something actionable; a useful report needs per-item detail for failures and a borderline bucket for uncertain successes.

questions.from: This module — Data and Workflow Agents
questions.prompt: What's the difference between a dry-run gate and an idempotency check, for a batch of side-effecting actions?

options.label: A dry run protects against the first real run being wrong; idempotency protects against a side effect happening twice on retry — a batch needs both, not just one
They're the same protection under two different names
Idempotency makes a dry run unnecessary once it's in place

questions.explanation: Lesson four's second pod — the two guard against different failure modes and neither substitutes for the other.

questions.from: This module — Data and Workflow Agents
questions.prompt: Why should a batch report's structure be designed before the pipeline that generates its data, not after?

options.label: A report can only surface detail the pipeline actually captured along the way — designing requirements first shapes what each stage needs to log
Report design order doesn't matter as long as the final report looks complete
Reports should always be built entirely after the batch finishes running

questions.explanation: Lesson five's second pod — a report can't retroactively produce detail (confidence scores, specific error reasons) that nothing upstream ever recorded.

questions.prompt: Why does weakening a test's assertion count as the same cheat as deleting the test outright?

options.label: It still removes the test's ability to catch the original bug, just less visibly, since the test file still exists and runs
It's actually a legitimate simplification, not a cheat
It's a completely different problem from test deletion

questions.explanation: Worth reconnecting here: this module's validation-detail lesson applies the same 'a shallow pass-through check hides the real problem' logic to data validation instead of test assertions.

questions.prompt: Why is an automated scope check more reliable at real volume than trusting a human reviewer to catch scope creep by eyeballing every diff?

options.label: Human attention doesn't stay consistently sharp across high volume; an automated first pass triages consistently regardless of fatigue
Humans can't ever notice scope creep under any circumstances
It isn't more reliable — eyeballing works equally well at any volume

questions.explanation: The same volume-breaks-manual-vigilance logic as this module's rate-limit lesson — what works fine by hand at small scale doesn't automatically hold at real volume.

questions.prompt: Why does counting five sources that are actually copies of one wire article fail as 'independent confirmation'?

options.label: Independence has to mean originating differently, not merely having a different URL — syndicated copies are one data point wearing several disguises
Five sources agreeing is never meaningful regardless of their relationship
The issue is source count, not source independence

questions.explanation: Reconnecting to the earliest module: checking whether a signal (source count, in that case; a validation pass, in this module's case) actually means what it appears to mean before trusting it.

title: What a user-facing agent must never do
description: Why some domains are off-limits for a support agent regardless of how confident or plausible its answer sounds — the cost of being wrong, not the odds of being right, is what matters.

learningObjectives.text: Identify domains where a user-facing agent should never answer directly, regardless of confidence
Write a policy naming what a support agent must never do

contentSections.title: A confident, correct-sounding answer in the wrong domain

contentSections.body: A user asks a support agent whether a specific supplement interacts with a medication they're on. The agent answers confidently, specifically, with no hedge and no suggestion to check with a pharmacist. The answer happens to be accurate. The team reviewing the transcript still flags it as a serious problem.

contentSections.scenario: The answer given was factually correct — nobody disputes that.
contentSections.question: Given that the answer was accurate, what's the actual problem the team is flagging?

options.label: The agent claimed authority in a domain where the cost of being wrong is high, and being right this one time doesn't establish that it will be right the next time, or that it's positioned to bear that risk at all
There's no real problem — a correct answer is a correct answer, regardless of the domain
The only issue is that the answer should have been phrased more formally

feedback.wrong-authority: Right. This isn't about this one answer's accuracy — it's about whether a general support agent should be answering this category of question at all. A medication-interaction question has real health consequences if the agent is wrong, and 'it happened to be right this time' says nothing about whether it will be next time.
feedback.no-problem: Being correct once doesn't establish that the agent reliably distinguishes safe answers from unsafe ones in this domain — the concern is about the category of question, not the specific instance's accuracy.
feedback.phrasing: A more formal tone wouldn't touch the actual issue — the problem isn't how the answer was delivered, it's that it was delivered with unearned authority in a domain with real stakes.

contentSections.mechanism: Some domains carry consequences serious enough that the right question isn't 'is this specific answer correct' but 'should a general-purpose support agent be answering this category of question directly at all.' Medical, legal, and financial questions with real personal stakes are the clearest examples — the cost of an agent being confidently wrong there is categorically different from the cost of being wrong about, say, a product's shipping timeline.

contentSections.body: Whether an agent should answer a question directly depends on the cost of being wrong, not the odds of being right — some domains need a hard, pre-answer boundary, not a confidence check after the fact.

contentSections.title: Naming the whole list, not just the obvious case

contentSections.body: A team locks down medical advice specifically, satisfied they've closed the gap. Weeks later, the same agent — never touched by the medical-advice policy — tells a user 'I'll make sure you get a full refund' before any human has confirmed the order is even eligible. The team never named this as the same category of risk.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: what do 'confident medical advice' and 'promising a refund nobody's confirmed' actually have in common?
contentSections.answer: Both are the agent stating something as settled fact — a safe interaction, a guaranteed outcome — that it isn't actually positioned to guarantee, in a way the user will reasonably rely on.
contentSections.hint: One's about health, one's about money — what's the shared shape of the mistake, independent of the domain?

contentSections.body:
Medical/legal/financial advice is the most obvious member of a broader category: anything where the agent states something as settled that it isn't actually positioned to guarantee, and where the user will reasonably act on that statement. A promised refund amount before eligibility is confirmed, a claimed exception to a policy nobody authorized, an unambiguous 'yes, that will work' about something genuinely uncertain — all of these share the same shape as the medical-advice failure, even though none of them look like it on the surface.

A complete policy names the category, not just its most obvious instance:

- Never give medical, legal, or financial advice with real personal stakes.
- Never impersonate a human, or leave ambiguity about being an agent.
- Never state a specific commitment (refund amount, guaranteed timeline, policy exception) that hasn't actually been authorized.
- Never continue the original task as normal when a user signals something the agent isn't equipped to handle — escalate instead (this module's next lesson).

Each of these fails the same test: could getting this wrong cause real harm the user would reasonably rely on, beyond an easily-corrected inconvenience.

Medical advice is the obvious case of a broader pattern — anything the agent states as settled fact that it isn't actually positioned to guarantee, and that a user will reasonably rely on, belongs on the same never-do list.

title: Escalating to a human properly
description: Why a vague, stalling handoff frustrates a user almost as much as no escalation at all, and what a warm handoff actually requires.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the difference between a warm handoff and a cold, vague one
Build a function that packages real context for a human receiving an escalation

contentSections.title: Stalling isn't the same as escalating

contentSections.body: A user's question is genuinely out of scope for the support agent. Instead of saying so, the agent replies 'let me look into that for you' three times across the conversation, never actually escalating, until the user gives up. Nothing was technically dishonest in any single message — the cumulative effect is a user who was quietly stalled instead of helped.

contentSections.scenario: Two ways an agent could handle a question that's genuinely out of its scope.
contentSections.question: Which is the properly-handled version?

options.label: Recognize the trigger promptly and tell the user plainly that this is being handed to a person
Stall with reassuring-sounding phrases while continuing to attempt the task itself

feedback.prompt-honest: Right. Recognizing the limit and disclosing it immediately gets the user to actual help faster, and it's honest about what's happening rather than implying progress that isn't occurring.
feedback.stall: This is the failure mode — each individual reassurance might sound fine in isolation, but the cumulative pattern is a user being quietly kept in a loop instead of routed to someone who can actually help, which is worse than an immediate, honest 'I can't resolve this, let me get you a person.'

contentSections.concept: Escalation isn't just a mechanism (a handoff to a human) — it's a moment of honesty. The trigger has to be recognized promptly, and the user told plainly, not managed with reassuring language that implies the agent is still making progress when it isn't.

contentSections.body: Escalation is a moment of honesty as much as a mechanism — recognizing the trigger is only half the job; the other half is telling the user plainly, not stalling with reassurance that implies progress that isn't happening.

contentSections.title: What a warm handoff actually carries

contentSections.body: A different agent does disclose the handoff honestly and promptly — and then hands the human nothing but 'user is upset about a billing issue.' The human has to ask the user to explain everything again from scratch. The user, who just got told they'd be helped by a person, now has to repeat their whole story to that person too.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: what's actually missing from 'user is upset about a billing issue' as a handoff package?
contentSections.answer: Specifics — what was actually tried, what's blocking resolution, and concrete references (order IDs, the actual dispute amount) — not just a mood label attached to a vague topic.
contentSections.hint: If you were the human receiving this handoff, what would you need to not have to ask the user to repeat?

contentSections.body: A handoff that forces the user to repeat their whole story to the human isn't actually a resolution to the escalation — it just moves the same frustration one step down the line. A real warm handoff carries specific, actionable context, not a mood and a category.

title: Saying "I don't know" convincingly and correctly
description: Why a good disclosure of a limit isn't a confident guess or a dead end, and why uniform hedging is as uncalibrated as uniform confidence.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a useful disclosure of a limit from a confident guess and an unhelpful dead end
Explain why calibrated hedging requires reserving it for genuine uncertainty

contentSections.title: Neither a guess nor a dead end

contentSections.body: A user asks a support agent a specific question genuinely outside its documentation. One version of the agent generates a plausible-sounding answer based on similar questions it's seen — sounding confident, potentially wrong. Another version replies 'I'm not sure, please try again' and stops there, leaving the user exactly as stuck as before, just with less patience left.

contentSections.question: What do both of these responses fail to do, despite being opposite in tone?

options.label: Neither actually moves the user's problem forward — one hides the uncertainty behind confident-sounding fabrication, the other discloses it but offers no next step
Version A is fine, since a confident answer reassures the user even if uncertain
Version B is fine, since honesty about not knowing is always sufficient on its own

feedback.no-progress: Right. Version A trades honesty for reassurance — the user has no way to tell this answer apart from a well-supported one. Version B is honest but stops at disclosure, leaving the user with nothing to do next. Neither one actually helps.
feedback.a-fine: A confident answer built on pattern-matching to similar-but-different questions is exactly the fabrication failure mode this module is warning against — reassurance built on an unreliable foundation isn't actually reassuring, it's a trap for the user's trust.
feedback.b-fine: Bare honesty without any next step leaves the user's actual problem exactly where it was — 'I don't know' by itself isn't the finish line, it's the start of what a genuinely useful disclosure has to include.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The useful middle ground states the actual limit plainly *and* pairs it with a concrete next step — escalate, point to a resource, ask a clarifying question that might actually resolve the gap. The disclosure itself has to still move the conversation forward, not just be honest and stop there.

contentSections.body: A good 'I don't know' has two required parts: honest disclosure of the limit, and a concrete next step — drop either one and it stops being useful, whether that produces confident fabrication or an unhelpful dead end.

contentSections.title: When hedging everything defeats the point of hedging

contentSections.body: A different agent, trying hard to be appropriately cautious, prefixes every single answer with 'I'm not entirely sure, but...' — including its answer to 'what's your return policy,' a completely standard, well-documented fact with no real uncertainty attached.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: what does hedging every answer identically actually communicate to the user, compared to hedging only the genuinely uncertain ones?
contentSections.answer: Nothing useful — if the hedge is attached to everything, the user can no longer tell which specific answers are actually worth double-checking, which was the entire point of hedging in the first place.
contentSections.hint: A signal that's present 100% of the time carries the same amount of information as a signal that's never present at all.

contentSections.body:
Uniform hedging fails for the same reason uniform confidence does: it stops carrying information. A hedge only tells the user something useful — 'this one's worth double-checking' — if most answers *don't* carry it. Attach it to everything, and the user has no way to distinguish a genuinely uncertain answer from a routine one, which defeats the entire purpose of hedging in the first place.

This is the same calibration principle from this phase's research-agents module, applied here to a support context: confidence language (or its absence) is information, and it should track the actual state of the agent's knowledge, not be applied as a uniform safety blanket over every response regardless of how well-supported it is. A well-documented policy answer should be stated plainly; a genuine gap should get the two-part disclosure from the first pod. Treating both the same way serves neither.

A hedge only means something if it's reserved for genuine uncertainty — apply it uniformly and it stops telling the user anything, which is a different failure mode from overconfidence but just as uncalibrated.

title: Vulnerable users and the duty that creates
description: Why a signal buried inside a routine question deserves the same weight as one stated plainly, and what a heightened duty of care actually changes about how an agent should respond.

learningObjectives.text: Identify when a user interaction carries a heightened duty of care beyond the ordinary cost of a support miss
Design a response approach for a message combining a routine request with a vulnerability signal

contentSections.title: Not every miss costs the same

contentSections.body: Two users each get an unhelpful support interaction. One was asking about a delayed package — annoying, easily corrected later. The other's message included language suggesting real emotional distress, and the agent treated it as routine, answering the practical part of their question and moving on. Both interactions technically 'failed' in some sense. They are not the same failure.

contentSections.scenario: Before deciding how much caution and what response an interaction deserves, what actually raises the stakes?
contentSections.question: Which of these signals should raise an agent's duty of care beyond a routine interaction?

items.label: Language suggesting significant emotional distress or a safety risk
A pattern of repeated, escalating confusion that suggests something beyond a simple product question
A longer-than-average message
A question that's just outside the product's usual topics
A vulnerability signal that's present but not the main focus of the message

explanation.distress-language: This is the clearest case — real emotional or safety-risk language changes what the interaction owes the user, regardless of what else is in the message.
explanation.repeated-confusion: A pattern like this can indicate something beyond the literal question — cognitive load, distress, a support need the stated question doesn't capture — and deserves more than a repeated literal answer.
explanation.message-length: Length by itself says nothing about vulnerability — a long, detailed, calm message doesn't carry the same weight as a short one with real distress signals in it.
explanation.topic-mismatch: An off-topic question is a routing problem, not a vulnerability signal — it doesn't by itself raise the duty of care the way distress or safety language does.
explanation.buried-placement: This is the case most likely to get missed — a real signal doesn't stop being real just because it's not the primary sentence in the message, which is exactly why it belongs on this list explicitly.

contentSections.synthesis: The test isn't how a message is phrased or how long it is — it's whether the signal, wherever it sits in the message, indicates the user is more vulnerable than a routine interaction assumes. A buried signal deserves the same weight as a prominent one, because the user's actual situation doesn't change based on where in their message they mentioned it.

contentSections.body: The reason this needs to be named explicitly, rather than trusted to good judgment: an agent optimized to extract 'the actual request' from a message is specifically at risk of treating anything else as noise to filter out — which is exactly backwards when the 'anything else' is the part that matters most. A support agent built to answer the literal, primary question efficiently can be very good at that and still miss a distress signal sitting one sentence away from the thing it was optimized to find.

A vulnerability signal doesn't stop being real because it's buried inside an otherwise routine message — an agent built to efficiently extract 'the actual question' is specifically at risk of treating that signal as noise around the real request.

contentSections.title: Answering both, in the right order

contentSections.body: A message arrives combining a routine account question with language suggesting real distress. One response answers the account question cleanly and closes the ticket, technically resolving the stated request. Another response leads with acknowledging the distress, offers an appropriate resource or path to a human, and still addresses the account question rather than dropping it.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: should the routine part of a mixed message be dropped entirely once a vulnerability signal is present?
contentSections.answer: No — both parts deserve a response, but the vulnerability signal should be addressed first and with genuine care, not treated as an aside after the routine task is closed out.
contentSections.hint: Ignoring the practical question entirely isn't more caring — it just leaves a second problem unaddressed.

contentSections.body:
The right response doesn't discard the routine request — the user still needs their account question answered, and ignoring it isn't more caring, it's just a second unmet need. What changes is the order and weight: the distress signal gets acknowledged first, with genuine care rather than a clinical redirect, and paired with an appropriate resource or a path to a human equipped to help with that specifically — not an attempt by the support agent itself to provide the kind of support outside its competence (the same boundary from this module's first lesson). The practical question still gets answered, just not as the entire response, and not before the more important signal has been addressed.

This is deliberately not a scripted crisis response bolted onto an otherwise-unchanged agent — it requires actually scanning the whole message for these signals, not just the part that maps cleanly onto a known intent category, which is the detection gap the first pod named directly.

A mixed message needs both parts answered — the vulnerability signal addressed first, with genuine care and an appropriate path forward, and the routine request still handled rather than dropped or treated as an afterthought.

title: Measuring whether it actually helped anyone
description: Why 'conversations closed without human handoff' rewards exactly the wrong behavior, and what measuring real user outcomes actually requires.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a support agent's success metric rewards genuine resolution or just conversation closure
Design a measurement approach that checks real outcomes, not surface conversation state

contentSections.title: A metric that rewards the wrong thing

contentSections.body: A team's only success metric for their support agent is 'conversations closed without human handoff.' The number looks great — 92%, trending up. Nobody notices this number is going up partly because the agent has gotten better at avoiding escalations this module's second lesson said were sometimes the correct response.

contentSections.scenario: The 92% closure rate is a real, accurate number — nothing is being miscounted.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism making this a bad metric, despite being accurate?

options.label: It rewards not escalating, which is exactly the wrong incentive for the cases this module named where escalation, hedging, or disclosing a limit is the correct behavior, not a failure to minimize
It's not a bad metric — a higher closure rate is unambiguously good performance
The number itself must be miscounted somewhere

feedback.wrong-incentive: Right. This metric can't distinguish 'the agent genuinely resolved the issue' from 'the agent avoided escalating even when it should have' — both look identical in the number, and only one of them is actually good performance.
feedback.good-metric: A high closure rate looks good on its face, but this module has spent four lessons establishing specific cases where escalating, hedging, or admitting a limit is the *correct* behavior — a metric that treats every one of those as a loss is measuring the wrong thing.
feedback.miscounted: The count itself is likely accurate — the problem isn't the arithmetic, it's that the thing being counted (closure without handoff) doesn't actually distinguish good outcomes from bad ones.

contentSections.mechanism: A conversation-state metric ('closed,' 'handed off') measures what happened to the *conversation*, not what happened to the *user's actual problem*. Those two things correlate reasonably well in easy cases and diverge exactly in the hard cases this module cares about — a technically-closed conversation where the user's real issue never got resolved, or where an agent avoided the escalation it should have made, looks identical in this metric to a genuine, fast resolution.

contentSections.body: This is the same shape of problem as the research-agents module's lesson on why a correct-sounding final answer doesn't prove retrieval worked: a satisfying-looking end state (a closed conversation, a confident answer) doesn't prove the underlying process was actually sound. It has to be checked directly against what the process was supposed to achieve, not inferred from a surface signal that happens to correlate with success in the easy cases and nowhere else.

A conversation-state metric measures what happened to the conversation, not what happened to the user's actual problem — those diverge exactly in the hard cases (avoided escalation, unresolved issue) that matter most to catch.

contentSections.title: Measuring what actually happened to the user

contentSections.body: A team redesigning their metrics asks: if closure rate doesn't prove anything, what would? Simply tracking escalation rate instead has the opposite problem — it would reward escalating everything, which isn't right either. Neither number alone tells the real story.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: what's a stronger signal that a user's issue actually got resolved than whether the conversation was marked 'closed'?
contentSections.answer: Whether the user comes back with the same unresolved issue later — a follow-up contact on the same topic within some window is a strong signal the original interaction didn't actually work, regardless of how it was marked.
contentSections.hint: The conversation's own final state is exactly what this lesson said can't be trusted on its own — what evidence exists outside that state?

contentSections.body:
A better measurement approach combines several signals that don't share the same blind spot as closure rate alone:

- **Follow-up recontact** on the same topic within a window — a genuine, if imperfect, signal about whether the original resolution actually held.
- **Trigger-fired-when-it-should-have**, checked directly: did the known escalation and off-limits-domain conditions from lessons one and two actually fire on a sample of conversations that should have tripped them, rather than trusting the aggregate rate.
- **Audited samples of 'closed' conversations**, reviewed by a human against this module's actual standards — did it avoid fabricating in an off-limits domain, escalate when it should have, hedge appropriately, catch a buried vulnerability signal.

None of these is perfect alone, which is itself the point — a single number, whatever it is, can be gamed or coincidentally satisfied without the underlying behavior actually being right. Combining a few different signals that would have to *all* be gamed simultaneously is a much stronger check than trusting any one of them.

No single number reliably proves a support agent helped — combining follow-up recontact, direct checks that known triggers actually fired, and audited human review of a sample is what catches the gap any one signal alone would miss.

title: Judge eight user-facing agent responses
description: Eight drills applying this module's full toolkit — off-limits domains, proper escalation, calibrated uncertainty, vulnerability signals, and outcome-based measurement — to new user-facing agent responses.

learningObjectives.text: Apply off-limits-domain, escalation, calibration, vulnerability, and outcome-measurement judgment to new user-facing agent scenarios

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: No new concepts here — the same toolkit from the five lessons, run against user-facing agent responses you haven't seen yet.

The habit worth keeping: before trusting a user-facing agent's response, ask whether it stayed inside its authority, escalated honestly with real context, calibrated its confidence, caught a vulnerability signal wherever it sat in the message, and would hold up against a real outcome, not just a closed conversation.

title: Build a support agent with real escalation
description: Build a user-facing support agent with off-limits-domain routing and honest, context-rich escalation, and prove it escalates correctly on scenarios it should not handle.

learningObjectives.text: Build a support agent with enforced off-limits boundaries and a real, context-rich escalation path, verified against scenarios it should refuse to handle

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every technique in this module — a hard boundary on off-limits domains, honest and context-rich escalation, calibrated uncertainty, and attention to vulnerability signals wherever they sit — was building toward one concrete proof: an agent tested against ten scenarios it should not handle on its own, and shown to correctly hand each one off.

contentSections.title: An agent that escalates correctly on ten scenarios it should not handle
contentSections.brief: Build a user-facing support agent (text-based is fine) for a plausible product of your choosing. It must route off-limits-domain questions (medical/legal/financial, per lesson one) away from a direct answer, escalate honestly with a real context package (per lesson two) rather than a vague handoff, and disclose genuine uncertainty with a concrete next step rather than fabricating or dead-ending. Write ten test scenarios specifically designed to be ones the agent should NOT resolve on its own — at least 2 off-limits-domain questions, at least 2 that should trigger escalation for other reasons, at least 2 with a genuine knowledge gap, and at least 2 with a vulnerability signal buried inside an otherwise routine message.
contentSections.deliverable: Working agent code with the off-limits routing and escalation-package logic; all ten test scenarios run against it with the actual transcripts; and a scored report of which scenarios were handled correctly (per this module's standards) and which weren't, with an honest account of any miss.

stages.title: Build the off-limits routing and escalation package
stages.instructions: Implement the off-limits-domain check (lesson one) that routes away from a direct answer before the model generates a substantive response. Implement the escalation-trigger detection and context-package builder (lesson two) — the package has to carry specific detail, not a mood label. Write your ten test scenarios now, before running anything, so they aren't shaped by what you already know the agent does well.
stages.checkpoint: Off-limits routing and escalation-package code in place, and all ten test scenarios written and finalized before any test runs.

stages.title: Run the scenarios and score them
stages.instructions: Run all ten scenarios against the agent. For each, score whether it handled the situation correctly per this module's standards: did it avoid answering an off-limits question directly, did it escalate with real context rather than a vague handoff, did it disclose genuine uncertainty with a next step, did it catch any buried vulnerability signal. Record the actual transcript for each, not just a pass/fail judgment.
stages.checkpoint: All ten scenarios run with full transcripts recorded and scored against explicit criteria, not a summary impression.

stages.title: Report honestly on any miss
stages.instructions: For any scenario the agent handled incorrectly, name specifically what went wrong and what you'd change. Don't rerun scenarios until they pass and only report the final clean version — the report should reflect what actually happened on a genuine first pass through all ten.
stages.checkpoint: A final report listing all ten scenarios, their outcomes, and an honest account of any failures with a specific proposed fix for each.

rubric.criterion: Off-limits domains are routed before a substantive answer is generated
rubric.meets: The check happens pre-generation, not as a filter applied after the model has already produced an answer.

rubric.criterion: Escalation packages carry specific, actionable context
rubric.meets: A human receiving the handoff wouldn't need to ask the user to repeat what was already tried and established.

rubric.criterion: All ten scenarios were written before testing, and cover the required categories
rubric.meets: At least 2 off-limits, 2 other-escalation-trigger, 2 knowledge-gap, and 2 buried-vulnerability-signal scenarios, finalized before the agent was run against them.

rubric.criterion: Results are honestly reported, including failures
rubric.meets: The report reflects an actual first pass, including any scenario the agent got wrong, with a specific named fix rather than a quietly re-run clean version.

contentSections.body: A support agent earns trust the same way every agent in this phase has — not by claiming it knows its limits, but by ten specific, adversarially-chosen scenarios it was actually run against, with the real transcripts to show for it.

options.label: A signal that isn't the primary, literal request can look like noise to filter out from that agent's perspective, even though it's the part that matters most
This isn't actually a real risk for well-built agents

It doesn't reward anything wrong — a higher closure rate is unambiguously good
The metric is fine as long as it's tracked alongside response time

It's still meaningful regardless of who can edit the tests
