questions.explanation: Reconnecting further back: a verification signal (a green suite, a closed conversation) is only as trustworthy as its independence from the thing it's supposed to be checking.

title: Choosing a task that justifies an agent
description: Why 'automation is always an improvement' is false — and the honest cost-benefit check a capstone task has to survive before any code gets written.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a task's volume, stakes, and ambiguity actually justify the cost of building an agent
Apply a checklist for choosing a genuinely agent-shaped task

contentSections.title: Automation isn't free just because it's possible

contentSections.body: A team proposes an agent to draft their weekly internal status report — a task a person currently does by hand in about 15 minutes, rarely with errors. It's technically straightforward to build. The team pauses before starting: is this actually worth building?

contentSections.scenario: The task is technically automatable, and the agent would probably work.
contentSections.question: What's the actual argument against building it, even though it's technically feasible?

options.label: The task is already cheap and reliable by hand, so an agent's real cost — the guardrails, verification, and monitoring this whole track has spent four modules establishing — likely exceeds a 15-minute, low-error task's upside
Agents should never be used for report-generation tasks under any circumstances
There's no real argument against it — if it's technically possible, it should be built

feedback.cost-benefit: Right. This isn't a rule against reports specifically — it's the actual arithmetic. An agent that does this task well still costs real engineering and ongoing verification effort, and a task with almost no room to improve has very little upside to offset that cost.
feedback.blanket-no: The objection isn't to the task category — a high-volume, error-prone, ambiguous version of a similar task might be a great fit for an agent. The objection is specific to this task's actual profile: low volume, low stakes, already fast and accurate.
feedback.always-build: Technical feasibility and worthwhile investment are different questions — this whole track has been about the real cost of building an agent responsibly, and that cost doesn't disappear just because the task is easy to automate.

contentSections.mechanism: Every technique in this track — verification, guardrails, review gates, monitoring — has a real cost to build and maintain. That cost is roughly constant regardless of the task; what varies is the benefit. A high-volume, high-stakes, or genuinely ambiguous task can easily justify that cost. A fast, already-accurate, low-volume task usually can't — the guardrails cost more than the task was ever worth.

contentSections.body:
This is the first decision a capstone has to survive, and it's deliberately the same question a hiring manager or a team lead should ask before greenlighting any agent project — because the honest answer is sometimes no, and being able to say so is itself a skill this track has been building toward. A rough checklist:

1. Is the task high-volume or high-stakes enough that guardrail cost pays for itself?
2. Does it require genuine judgment under ambiguity, or is it actually deterministic (script-shaped, not agent-shaped)?
3. Can the cost of a wrong output be bounded without losing most of the benefit?
4. Is there an objective way to measure success, or would 'it seems fine' be the only available signal?
5. What does the current manual/existing version actually cost — is that cost real enough to be worth solving?

A task that fails most of these — like the status report — is a legitimate answer to 'don't build this,' not a failure to find something to build.
Technical feasibility and worthwhile investment are different questions — a task with little room to improve rarely justifies the real, ongoing cost of the guardrails a responsible agent needs.

contentSections.title: What a genuinely agent-shaped task looks like

contentSections.body: The same team considers a different task: triaging incoming support tickets by urgency and routing them to the right team. High volume, genuine judgment involved (urgency isn't always keyword-detectable), and a bounded cost if it's wrong (a ticket goes to the wrong team, correctable, not catastrophic).

contentSections.question: Before reading on: using the same checklist from the first pod, is ticket triage a stronger or weaker candidate than the status report task?
contentSections.answer: Stronger — it has real volume and genuine ambiguity requiring judgment, both of which the report task lacked, and a wrong output is correctable rather than catastrophic.
contentSections.hint: Compare the two tasks directly against the checklist's five questions, one at a time.

contentSections.body:
This is the contrast worth internalizing before choosing a capstone task: volume and genuine ambiguity are the two strongest signals that a task is actually agent-shaped, not just automatable. A task that's mostly 'if X then do Y' with no real judgment involved is often better served by a simpler rule-based tool — which carries far less of the verification and guardrail burden this track has covered, and is often more reliable for exactly that reason.

Choosing a capstone task well means resisting the pull toward whatever's easiest to build a demo of, in favor of something that actually earns the cost of doing it properly — with real verification, real review gates, and real controls, the way this whole track has taught.

Volume and genuine judgment-under-ambiguity are the two strongest signals a task is actually agent-shaped — a task with neither is often better served by a simpler tool than by carrying the full weight of agentic guardrails.

title: Designing for verification from the start
description: Why an eval set built after the agent already exists tests a moving target, and what defining success criteria first actually requires.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why defining success criteria before building the agent produces a more honest evaluation
Build an eval set including deliberately hard and ambiguous cases, not just easy confirmations

contentSections.title: An eval set that tests a moving target

contentSections.body: A team builds their ticket-triage agent first, gets it working reasonably well on the examples they tried while developing it, and only then sits down to write an eval set — drawing test cases from the same examples they'd already been using to tune the prompt. The eval passes at 94%. Real production traffic performs far worse.

contentSections.scenario: Two different orders for building an agent and its evaluation.
contentSections.question: Which order produces a more honest evaluation?

options.label: Define success criteria and build the eval set before tuning the agent against it
Build and tune the agent first, then write an eval set based on what it already does

feedback.eval-first: Right. An eval set defined before the agent exists (or before it's tuned) tests against independent success criteria — it can't accidentally be shaped around whatever the agent happens to already do well.
feedback.agent-first: This is the pattern that produced the 94%-on-eval, worse-in-production gap — an eval set built from examples already used to tune the agent tests a moving target that quietly matches the agent's existing behavior, not real success criteria.

contentSections.concept: The order matters because an eval set is only informative if it's independent of the thing it's evaluating. Writing it after the agent already exists, especially from the same examples used during development, risks it becoming a confirmation of what the agent already does rather than a genuine test of whether it does the right thing.

contentSections.body:
This is the same principle as the coding-agents module's test-integrity lesson, applied to evaluation design instead of unit tests: a check only means something if it's independent of the thing being checked. A test suite an agent can edit stops proving anything; an eval set shaped by what the agent already does has the same problem, just with the causality reversed — instead of the agent bending the check, the *builder* unconsciously bent the check toward the agent.

In practice: write the eval set — real test cases with a labeled correct answer, decided independently, before or very early in development — and treat later agent iterations as things being measured against that fixed target, not the other way around.

A check only means something if it's independent of the thing it's checking — an eval set has to be defined before, and independent of, the agent it will measure, or it risks confirming the agent's existing behavior instead of testing it.

contentSections.title: Writing cases that could actually reveal a weakness

contentSections.body: A team does write their eval set independently — but every case is a clean, unambiguous example: an obviously-critical ticket, an obviously-low-urgency one. The agent scores 98%. None of the 40 cases resembled the messy, borderline tickets that make up most of real traffic.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: what's missing from an eval set made entirely of clean, unambiguous cases?
contentSections.answer: Deliberately hard and borderline cases — the ones genuinely close to the line between two categories, which is exactly where an agent is most likely to actually fail, and exactly what a clean-cases-only eval set never tests.
contentSections.hint: Real production traffic is rarely as clean as a textbook example — does an eval set built only from textbook examples tell you anything about the messy cases?

contentSections.body:
An eval set of only easy, clear-cut cases produces a number that looks reassuring and predicts almost nothing about real performance, because real traffic is disproportionately made of exactly the messy, borderline cases a clean eval never includes. A genuinely useful eval set deliberately includes:

- **Deliberately tricky cases** — ones with a surface feature that might mislead a model (e.g. a ticket mentioning 'week-long' problem that's actually low-urgency, tempting a model to over-weight duration).
- **Genuinely ambiguous cases**, explicitly marked as such — where even a careful human reviewer might reasonably disagree, scored more leniently or reviewed separately rather than pretending there's one right answer.
- **Category-representative coverage**, not just volume — especially for the highest-stakes category, even if it's rare in raw frequency, because getting that category wrong matters more than the aggregate number can show (this module's next lesson goes further into why).

```
{ ticketText, correctUrgency, whyThisLevel, isAmbiguous: bool }
```

An eval set built this way produces a number that actually predicts something about production, instead of a reassuring number that predicts nothing.

An eval set made only of clean, easy cases produces a reassuring number that predicts almost nothing about production — deliberately including hard, borderline, and category-representative cases is what makes the eval actually informative.

title: Building, evaluating and iterating on evidence
description: Why a satisfying upward accuracy trend can hide a systematic, high-stakes weakness — and how a category breakdown catches what an aggregate number can't.

learningObjectives.text: Analyze whether an improving aggregate eval score is safe to trust without a category-level breakdown
Evaluate a category-level breakdown to identify where iteration should actually focus

contentSections.title: A rising number that stops telling you anything

contentSections.body: A team's ticket-triage agent scores 62% on the eval set, then 68% after one prompt tweak, then 71% after another. Satisfied with the upward trend, they stop iterating and prepare to ship. Nobody has looked at what's actually still failing in the remaining 29%.

contentSections.scenario: Before seeing the real breakdown: given an aggregate 71% score across four urgency categories (low, medium, high, critical), how evenly would you guess that 29% of failures is distributed across categories, on a typical real dataset like this?
contentSections.question: Your estimate — how concentrated (versus evenly spread) is the failure rate likely to be across categories?
contentSections.explanation: Very concentrated, not evenly spread, is the typical real pattern — failures on a task like urgency triage tend to cluster in the hardest, most consequential category (often the rarest one, 'critical'), not distribute evenly. An aggregate score blends a category performing at 95% with one performing at 35%, and the blended number alone gives no hint which is which.

contentSections.body: An aggregate score blends every category into one number — a category-level breakdown is what actually reveals whether a rising trend is safe to stop iterating on, or hiding a weak spot exactly where it matters most.

contentSections.title: Iterating on the actual gap, not the average

contentSections.body: The breakdown reveals it: 95% on low, 88% on medium, 60% on high, 35% on critical. The team's first instinct is another round of general prompt tweaking, the same kind that moved the aggregate from 62% to 71%.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: is more general prompt tweaking (the same kind that worked for the aggregate number) the right next move here?
contentSections.answer: No — the category breakdown points at a specific, concentrated problem (critical-ticket classification), which needs targeted investigation into that category specifically, not another round of general tweaking that already produced diminishing aggregate returns.
contentSections.hint: Would a general tweak that improves the easy categories slightly move the needle on a category that's already failing 65% of the time?

contentSections.body:
Once a weak spot is identified this specifically, the next step changes: investigate the critical-ticket failures directly — are they systematically under-classified as 'high' (a directional, likely fixable bias, maybe a specific missing signal in the prompt), or scattered with no pattern (a harder, more fundamental gap, maybe needing more or better examples of what critical actually looks like)? This is real diagnostic work, not another blind prompt tweak-and-rerun cycle.

This closes the loop on why lesson two's eval design matters: a category breakdown is only possible if the eval set had enough labeled critical-category examples to break down in the first place. An eval set that skipped the rare, high-stakes category (or lumped everything into one aggregate number by design) would never have surfaced this gap — the ability to iterate on real evidence depends entirely on the evidence having been built to support it.

Once a weak spot is identified by category, the next move is targeted diagnosis of that specific gap — not another round of the general tweaking that already produced diminishing returns on the aggregate.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the specific risk each deployment control (cost cap, kill switch, monitoring) guards against
Design concrete deployment controls for a specific agent

contentSections.title: Three ways a good eval score doesn't protect you

contentSections.body: A team's agent passes its eval set at a strong, category-balanced 89% and gets deployed with nothing else in place — no cost cap, no kill switch, no monitoring beyond what the eval already showed. A week later, an unexpected input pattern sends it into a tool-calling loop that runs for six hours before anyone notices the bill.

contentSections.scenario: The eval score itself was genuinely strong and honestly measured, per this module's earlier lessons.
contentSections.question: What's the actual gap that let this happen, given the eval was legitimately good?

options.label: An eval score measures accuracy on the test cases it covers — it says nothing about what happens on an unexpected input in production, or what stops a runaway process once one starts
The eval score must have been fabricated or the process wouldn't have failed
Nothing could have prevented this — deployed agents are inherently unpredictable

feedback.eval-doesnt-cover-runtime: Right. An eval set, however well-designed, tests behavior on the cases it contains — it has no mechanism for bounding what happens on an input nobody anticipated, or for stopping a process that's already gone wrong. That's a different, additional layer of protection.
feedback.fake-eval: Nothing here suggests the eval itself was dishonest — a genuinely good eval score and a genuinely unprotected runtime failure can coexist, because they're answering different questions.
feedback.unpreventable: A kill switch, a step limit, and cost monitoring are all specific, buildable protections against exactly this kind of runaway scenario — this isn't an unavoidable cost of deploying agents, it's a gap in what was actually built.

contentSections.mechanism: An eval score answers 'how accurate is this agent on the cases I tested.' It doesn't answer 'what happens on a case I didn't test' or 'what stops this from running away once something goes wrong.' Those require dedicated, separate controls — this lesson's whole point is that a strong eval score is necessary but nowhere near sufficient for safe deployment.

contentSections.body:
Three specific risks, three specific controls — not general reassurance, but concrete mechanisms:

1. **Runaway cost** — a hard spend cap enforced by the harness itself (not a billing alert that fires after the money is already spent), which halts new runs once crossed.
2. **Unbounded/runaway behavior** — a kill switch simple and fast enough to trigger under pressure (an admin toggle checked at the start of every run, not a multi-step deploy process), plus a hard per-request step or token limit that caps how far any single run can go before it's forced to stop.
3. **Silent failure** — monitoring frequent enough to catch a problem before it compounds (hourly error-rate checks, not just a daily summary), so a degrading pattern gets caught early rather than discovered a week later in a bill.

A strong eval score answers 'how accurate on the cases I tested' — it says nothing about an unanticipated input or a runaway process, which need their own dedicated, concrete controls: a cost cap, a kill switch and step limit, and frequent monitoring.

contentSections.title: Building the controls for your own agent

contentSections.body: A team building their own capstone-style agent writes 'we'll monitor it and add limits if needed' in their deployment notes — a plan to add controls reactively, after something goes wrong, rather than having them in place from the first real run.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: what's the risk of a plan to 'add controls if something goes wrong,' compared to having them in place from the start?
contentSections.answer: The first real incident happens with no protection in place — a kill switch or cost cap added reactively only helps for the second runaway event, not the one that revealed the need for it.
contentSections.hint: A control that exists 'if needed' by definition doesn't exist during the exact event that would have needed it.

contentSections.body: Controls added reactively protect against the second incident, not the first — the concrete deliverable is specific, working thresholds in place before the first real run, not a stated intention to add them later.

title: Defending the design under challenge
description: Why a specific challenge deserves a specific answer naming the actual mechanism — not a general appeal to overall quality, and not defensiveness about a fair question.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a defense of an agent's design actually answers the specific challenge raised
Construct a genuine, specific defense of a design choice under direct challenge

contentSections.title: A specific question deserves a specific answer

contentSections.body: In a design review, someone asks a presenter: 'what happens if this agent is confidently wrong on a critical-urgency ticket and nobody catches it for a week?' The presenter answers by citing their eval set's strong 89% overall accuracy. The question goes unanswered.

contentSections.scenario: The 89% accuracy figure is real and honestly measured.
contentSections.question: What's actually wrong with using it as the answer to this specific question?

options.label: It answers a different question — the challenge is about a specific failure scenario, and overall accuracy says nothing about which control would catch or bound that particular case
Nothing is wrong — a strong accuracy number is always a sufficient answer to any challenge about the system
The number itself must be too low to be a good answer

feedback.different-question: Right. This is the same gap as citing a batch report's aggregate success rate when someone asks about a specific category of failure — a good overall number doesn't tell you what happens in one particular bad-case scenario, and this challenge is specifically about that scenario.
feedback.sufficient: A challenge naming a specific failure mode is asking what stops or limits *that* scenario specifically — an aggregate number, however strong, doesn't address it, no matter how high it is.
feedback.too-low: The number's value isn't the issue here — even a 99% accuracy figure wouldn't answer 'what specifically catches this one bad case,' because it's the wrong kind of evidence for the question being asked.

contentSections.mechanism: This track has repeatedly shown that an aggregate or surface-level metric can hide exactly the failure that matters most — a batch report's success rate, a support agent's closure rate, an eval's blended average. The same principle applies under a design challenge: a specific 'what happens if X' question needs a specific answer naming the actual mechanism (a review gate, an alert threshold, a bounded blast radius) that addresses X, not a retreat to a comforting aggregate.

contentSections.body: A strong defense under challenge names the actual, concrete control: 'critical-urgency tickets specifically route through a mandatory human review gate before final action, regardless of the agent's confidence — so a wrong classification there gets caught before it causes harm, independent of the overall accuracy number.' That's an answer to the actual question asked. Citing the 89% figure again is not, however true it is.

A specific challenge about a specific failure scenario needs a specific answer naming the actual control that addresses it — an aggregate quality number, however strong, is a different kind of evidence and doesn't answer the question.

contentSections.title: Engaging with a fair challenge instead of deflecting it

contentSections.body: A different, harder challenge: 'your eval set was written by you, tested by you, and graded by you. Why should anyone trust that number?' One presenter gets defensive, insisting the number is trustworthy simply because real effort went into it. Another engages directly with what's actually being asked.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: is 'I put real effort into building this eval set' a genuine answer to a challenge about self-grading?
contentSections.answer: No — effort doesn't address the actual concern, which is about independence, not diligence. A genuine answer has to name specific design choices that reduce (not eliminate) the self-grading risk.
contentSections.hint: The challenge is specifically about who's grading, not about how much work went into the eval — does effort answer a question about independence?

contentSections.body:
This is a genuinely fair challenge, and it deserves genuine engagement rather than defensiveness or a claim that the concern doesn't apply. A strong answer names specific things that make the eval harder to have unconsciously gamed even though it was self-authored: it was finalized before the agent was tuned against it (lesson two's principle), it deliberately includes adversarial and ambiguous cases rather than confirmatory ones, results are broken down by category rather than reported as one aggregate (so a hidden weak spot can't disappear into a good average, per lesson three) — and, honestly, naming what still isn't independently verified and what the next concrete step would be to strengthen that claim further.

The weakest response to a fair challenge is either defensiveness (treating the question as an attack rather than a legitimate concern) or overclaiming (insisting the number is simply trustworthy). The strongest response engages with the actual mechanism of the concern and is honest about what's still unresolved — which is, in miniature, the same standard this entire capstone module has been asking the learner's own agent to meet.

A fair challenge about self-grading deserves genuine engagement, not defensiveness or overclaiming — name the specific design choices that reduce the risk, and be honest about what's still unverified.

title: Answer seven hard challenges to your design
description: Seven drills applying this module's full toolkit — task justification, eval design, category-level iteration, deployment controls, and genuine challenge defense — to new capstone scenarios.

learningObjectives.text: Apply task-justification, eval-design, iteration, deployment-control, and challenge-defense judgment to new capstone scenarios

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: No new concepts here — the same toolkit from the five lessons, run against capstone-style design decisions and challenges you haven't seen yet.

The habit worth keeping, for every agent you build after this track: does the task actually justify the cost, was success defined before tuning began, does the evidence break down by what matters most rather than hiding behind an average, are the deployment controls concrete rather than promised, and can every design choice survive a specific, direct challenge.

title: Deliver the capstone agent
description: Bring together the whole track: build, evaluate, deploy with real controls, and defend an agent that does something genuinely worth building.

learningObjectives.text: Build, evaluate, deploy, and defend a complete agent, applying every module of this track's toolkit end to end

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This lab is the whole track, applied end to end, to one real agent you choose and build: a task that actually justifies an agent, an eval set defined before tuning began, real iteration guided by a category breakdown, deployment controls that exist before the first real run, and a written defence that can survive a specific challenge — not a demo, a deliverable someone else could actually rely on.

contentSections.title: A deployed agent with an eval set, measured results, cost per run, controls, and a written defence
contentSections.brief: Choose one agent to build — from any domain this track covered (research, coding, data/workflow, or user-facing support) or a genuine combination. It must pass the cost-benefit check from lesson one before you write any code. Build a real eval set, independent of the agent, before tuning it. Iterate using category-level analysis, not just an aggregate trend. Deploy it (a real, working deployment — even a simple always-on script or scheduled job counts, it doesn't need to be production infrastructure) with concrete cost limits, a kill switch, and monitoring in place from the start. Write a defence document addressing at least three specific, adversarial challenges to your design.
contentSections.deliverable: A working agent; an independent eval set with category-level results, including the honest category-by-category breakdown even where it's weak; documented, working deployment controls (cost cap, kill switch, monitoring) with the actual thresholds chosen and why; and a written defence answering at least three specific challenges with named mechanisms, not general reassurance.

stages.title: Justify the task
stages.instructions: Run your chosen task through lesson one's checklist explicitly — volume, stakes, ambiguity, boundable cost of error, measurability. Write this up as a short justification before building anything. If your first idea fails the checklist, choose a different task rather than building it anyway.
stages.checkpoint: A written task justification, explicitly addressing each checklist question, for a task that actually passes it.

stages.title: Build the eval set before the agent
stages.instructions: Write your eval set — real test cases with independently-decided correct answers, including deliberately hard and ambiguous cases and coverage of your highest-stakes category — before building or meaningfully tuning the agent (lesson two).
stages.checkpoint: A finalized eval set, written and reviewed before agent-tuning began, including at least a few deliberately hard cases per category.

stages.title: Build and iterate with category-level evidence
stages.instructions: Build the agent and run it against your eval set. Break results down by category, not just in aggregate (lesson three). Iterate at least once specifically targeting whatever category shows the weakest performance, and re-run to measure whether that targeted iteration actually helped.
stages.checkpoint: At least one full eval run with a category breakdown, plus one targeted iteration cycle with before/after numbers for the specific weak category.

stages.title: Deploy with real controls
stages.instructions: Set up a real (even if simple) deployment with concrete, working controls: a cost cap enforced in code, a kill switch, and monitoring on some real cadence (lesson four). Document the actual thresholds you chose and your reasoning for each.
stages.checkpoint: Working deployment controls with documented thresholds — not a description of what controls should exist, but code and numbers that actually exist.

stages.title: Write the defence
stages.instructions: Write a defence document addressing at least three specific, adversarial challenges to your design (at least one about a specific bad-case failure scenario, at least one about the trustworthiness of your self-authored eval set). Each answer must name a specific mechanism, not a general reassurance about overall quality (lesson five).
stages.checkpoint: A written defence with at least three specific challenge-and-answer pairs, each naming a concrete mechanism rather than an aggregate quality claim.

rubric.criterion: The task genuinely passes the cost-benefit checklist
rubric.meets: The justification explicitly addresses volume, stakes, ambiguity, boundable error cost, and measurability — not just an assertion that the task is worth automating.

rubric.criterion: The eval set predates meaningful agent tuning
rubric.meets: Test cases and their correct answers were finalized before the agent was tuned against them, and include deliberately hard/ambiguous cases, not just easy confirmations.

rubric.criterion: Iteration is guided by category-level evidence
rubric.meets: At least one iteration cycle specifically targets a category-level weakness identified in a breakdown, with before/after numbers for that category, not just an aggregate trend.

rubric.criterion: Deployment controls are real, not described
rubric.meets: A working cost cap, kill switch, and monitoring cadence actually exist, with documented thresholds and reasoning, before the first real run.

rubric.criterion: The defence answers specific challenges with specific mechanisms
rubric.meets: Each of the three-plus challenges gets an answer naming an actual control or design choice, not a retreat to an aggregate quality number or a defensive non-answer.

contentSections.body: This capstone is the whole track in miniature: a task worth building, evidence gathered honestly before it could be shaped by the agent it's testing, iteration guided by where it actually matters, controls that exist before they're needed, and a defence that names real mechanisms — the same standard every module in this phase has been building toward, applied once, completely, to something real.

description: Ungraded retrieval: 4 from this module, 4 from Agents That Talk to People (the previous module in this phase), 2 from further back in Data and Workflow Agents.

learningObjectives.text: Recall this module's capstone vocabulary and reconnect it across the whole phase's guardrail and verification principles

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Capstone — An Agent Worth Trusting
contentSections.framing: No grade, no timer. Answer from memory before scrolling back.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't a task's technical feasibility settle whether it's worth building an agent for?

options.label: An agent's real cost is the ongoing guardrails and verification it needs — a task with little room to improve may not have enough upside to offset that cost
Technical feasibility is always sufficient justification on its own
Feasibility and worth are the same question, just phrased differently

questions.explanation: Lesson one — the real cost of a responsibly-built agent is roughly constant regardless of the task, so the task's actual volume, stakes, and ambiguity are what determine whether that cost is worth paying.

questions.prompt: Why should an eval set be defined before an agent is tuned against it, rather than written afterward from examples already used during development?

options.label: An eval set written afterward risks being unconsciously shaped around what the agent already does well, testing a moving target instead of independent success criteria
Order doesn't matter as long as the eval set is eventually comprehensive
Writing the eval set afterward is always more accurate since more is known about the agent by then

questions.explanation: Lesson two — a check is only informative if it's independent of the thing it's checking; an eval set shaped by the agent's existing behavior risks confirming it rather than testing it.

questions.prompt: Why can a rising aggregate eval score (62% -> 68% -> 71%) still be unsafe to stop iterating on?

options.label: An aggregate blends every category into one number, so it can hide a severe, concentrated weakness in exactly the highest-stakes category
It can't — any consistent upward trend is sufficient evidence of readiness
The risk only applies to scores below 50%

questions.explanation: Lesson three — a category breakdown is what reveals whether a rising trend reflects broad improvement or a strong easy-category average masking a weak, high-stakes one.

questions.prompt: Why isn't a strong eval score, by itself, sufficient for safe deployment?

options.label: An eval score measures accuracy on the cases it covers — it says nothing about an unanticipated input or what stops a process that's already gone wrong
It is sufficient — a strong eval score is the only thing deployment safety depends on
Eval scores are unreliable in general and shouldn't be trusted for any purpose

questions.explanation: Lesson four — deployment needs its own dedicated controls (cost caps, kill switches, monitoring) because an eval score answers a different question than 'what happens at runtime on an unexpected input.'

questions.prompt: Why does citing an overall accuracy number fail to answer a challenge about one specific failure scenario?

options.label: The challenge asks what specific mechanism catches or bounds that scenario — an aggregate number is a different kind of evidence that doesn't address it, however strong it is
It doesn't fail — a strong enough accuracy number answers any challenge
It fails only if the accuracy number itself is below some threshold

questions.explanation: Lesson five — a specific challenge needs an answer naming the actual control that addresses that specific scenario, not a retreat to an aggregate quality claim.

questions.prompt: What's the strongest response to a fair challenge about a self-authored, self-graded eval set?

options.label: Naming specific design choices that reduce the self-grading risk (defined before tuning, adversarial cases included, category breakdown reported), and being honest about what's still unverified
Insisting the number is trustworthy because significant effort went into building the eval set
Treating the question as unfair and declining to engage with it

questions.explanation: Lesson five's second pod — genuine engagement naming concrete mechanisms, plus honesty about remaining gaps, beats both defensiveness and overclaiming.

questions.prompt: What are the two strongest signals that a task is genuinely agent-shaped, per this module's first lesson?

options.label: Real volume and genuine judgment required under ambiguity
Whether the task sounds impressive to automate
Whether the task can technically be done by an LLM at all

questions.explanation: Lesson one's second pod — volume and genuine ambiguity are what separate a task worth an agent's guardrail cost from one better served by a simpler tool or left manual.

questions.from: Previous module — Agents That Talk to People
questions.prompt: Why does 'conversations closed without human handoff' reward the wrong behavior as a support agent's success metric?

options.label: It rewards not escalating even when escalation was the correct response to the user's situation
It doesn't reward anything wrong — a higher closure rate is unambiguously good
The metric only fails when paired with a low response-time target

questions.explanation: Reconnecting to the previous module: the same 'a surface number can hide the failure that matters most' pattern as this module's eval-and-deployment lessons.

questions.from: Previous module — Agents That Talk to People
questions.prompt: What makes a handoff to a human 'warm' rather than cold and frustrating?

options.label: It carries specific, actionable context — what was tried, what's unresolved — so the user doesn't have to repeat their whole story
Simply disclosing that a human is taking over, regardless of what context travels with it
How fast the handoff happens, independent of what information is passed along

questions.explanation: The same specificity-over-vagueness principle as this module's defence lesson — a real answer, or a real handoff, needs concrete detail, not a category label.

questions.from: Older module — Data and Workflow Agents
questions.prompt: Why does a real-world side effect need its own idempotency check, separate from per-item computation-status tracking?

options.label: Redoing a computation is harmless, but redoing a side effect creates a second real-world event — the two need independent protection
Status tracking for computation already covers side effects automatically
Idempotency only matters for financial actions specifically

questions.explanation: Reconnecting further back: this module's deployment controls (kill switch, step limits) are the same category of deliberate, structural safeguard as idempotency — neither can be left to hope or good intentions.
